supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Let $\rho,\sigma:H\to H$ be self-adjoint linear maps with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one, and suppose every eigenvalue of $\sigma$ is strictly positive. Define $K_\sigma:=-\log\sigma$ by spectral calculus, and for any self-adjoint $\tau:H\to H$ with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one define $s(\tau):=-\operatorname{tr}(\tau\log\tau)=-\sum_{\lambda_j(\tau)>0}\lambda_j(\tau)\log\lambda_j(\tau)$, with the zero-eigenvalue term $0\log0:=0$ and natural logarithms, so the entropy is in nats. Define the modular-energy difference relative to $\sigma$ by $\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma):=\operatorname{tr}((\rho-\sigma)K_\sigma)$. Then

$$D(\rho\|\sigma)=\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma)-(s(\rho)-s(\sigma)).$$

For any nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ with $H=H_A\otimes H_B$, partial tracing both states over $H_B$ cannot increase relative entropy:

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\rho\|\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\sigma)\le D(\rho\|\sigma).$$

The identity and inequality are finite-dimensional mathematical statements; no Hamiltonian, physical energy, physical units, continuum limit, or gravitational entropy is assumed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: The finite Hilbert tensor product has product inner product and ordered product bases; the two-factor product basis is orthonormal.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: A linear map preserves the vector-space operations; an endomorphism is a linear map from a space to itself.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: Trace is the basis-independent finite sum of diagonal matrix entries, used for normalizations and trace pairings.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Let $\rho,\sigma:H\to H$ be self-adjoint linear maps with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one, and suppose every eigenvalue of $\sigma$ is strictly positive. Define $K_\sigma:=-\log\sigma$ by spectral calculus, and for any self-adjoint $\tau:H\to H$ with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one define $s(\tau):=-\operatorname{tr}(\tau\log\tau)=-\sum_{\lambda_j(\tau)>0}\lambda_j(\tau)\log\lambda_j(\tau)$, with the zero-eigenvalue term $0\log0:=0$ and natural logarithms, so the entropy is in nats. Define the modular-energy difference relative to $\sigma$ by $\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma):=\operatorname{tr}((\rho-\sigma)K_\sigma)$. Then

$$D(\rho\|\sigma)=\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma)-(s(\rho)-s(\sigma)).$$

For any nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ with $H=H_A\otimes H_B$, partial tracing both states over $H_B$ cannot increase relative entropy:

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\rho\|\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\sigma)\le D(\rho\|\sigma).$$

The identity and inequality are finite-dimensional mathematical statements; no Hamiltonian, physical energy, physical units, continuum limit, or gravitational entropy is assumed.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set. For each $\alpha\in I$, let $H_\alpha$ and $K_\alpha$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, and give

$$H_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}(H_\alpha\otimes K_\alpha)$$

the orthogonal direct-sum inner product: distinct summands are orthogonal and the inner product within a summand is the Hilbert tensor-product inner product. On elementary tensors that inner product is $\langle x\otimes y,x'\otimes y'\rangle=\langle x,x'\rangle\langle y,y'\rangle$. A map $T\otimes U$ acts by $(T\otimes U)(x\otimes y)=Tx\otimes Uy$, and a direct-sum map acts blockwise with zero off-diagonal blocks.

A complex-linear endomorphism is a linear map from a vector space to itself. A density matrix on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space is a self-adjoint endomorphism with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one; it is faithful when all eigenvalues are strictly positive. These are the conventions used for the finite density matrices in the earlier modular-balance result. The summand indexed by $\alpha$ is called the $\alpha$ sector. For each $\alpha$, fix a faithful density matrix $\chi_\alpha$ on $K_\alpha$. Let $\mathbf p=(p_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}$ satisfy $p_\alpha>0$ and $\sum_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha=1$, and let $\rho_\alpha$ be density matrices on $H_\alpha$. Define the encoded endomorphism

$$\mathcal E_\chi(\mathbf p,\rho):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha\,\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha.$$

When this encoded endomorphism is a density matrix, call it the encoded reduced state. The logical data are $\mathbf p$ and $\{\rho_\alpha\}$; the ancillary matrices $\{\chi_\alpha\}$ are held fixed. For a second strictly positive probability vector $\mathbf q$ and faithful density matrices $\sigma_\alpha$ on the same $H_\alpha$, write $\sigma_A:=\mathcal E_\chi(\mathbf q,\sigma)$ for the encoded reference endomorphism.

This is a finite-dimensional algebraic model. The definition makes no gravitational interpretation and does not identify a matrix entropy term with a geometric area.

derivations.claim: Choose orthonormal eigenbases for each $\rho_\alpha$, $\sigma_\alpha$, and $\chi_\alpha$ using [F2]. Write their eigenvalues as $r_{\alpha i}$, $t_{\alpha i}$, and $c_{\alpha j}$, respectively. In each block, the tensor products of the factor eigenvectors form an orthonormal basis and have eigenvalues $p_\alpha r_{\alpha i}c_{\alpha j}$ for $p_\alpha\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha$ and $q_\alpha t_{\alpha i}c_{\alpha j}$ for $q_\alpha\sigma_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha$. Thus every block is positive semidefinite, the finite orthogonal sum is positive semidefinite, and its trace is $\sum_\alpha p_\alpha(\sum_i r_{\alpha i})(\sum_j c_{\alpha j})=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha=1$; the same calculation with $q_\alpha,t_{\alpha i}$ proves $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_A=1$. Since $q_\alpha,t_{\alpha i},c_{\alpha j}$ are all strictly positive, every eigenvalue of $\sigma_A$ is positive, so the reference is faithful.

The eigenvalues of $\rho_A$ are exactly $p_\alpha r_{\alpha i}c_{\alpha j}$ over its orthogonal block eigenbases. Terms with $r_{\alpha i}=0$ contribute $0$ by the entropy convention; all other terms satisfy $\log(p_\alpha r_{\alpha i}c_{\alpha j})=\log p_\alpha+\log r_{\alpha i}+\log c_{\alpha j}$ by [F4]. Substituting in $s(\rho_A)$ and summing the finite products, using $\sum_i r_{\alpha i}=\sum_j c_{\alpha j}=1$, gives $s(\rho_A)=-\sum_\alpha p_\alpha\log p_\alpha+\sum_\alpha p_\alpha s(\rho_\alpha)+\sum_\alpha p_\alpha s(\chi_\alpha)$, which is the asserted entropy identity.

Write $u_{\alpha i}$ for the chosen eigenbasis of $\sigma_\alpha$ and $v_{\alpha j}$ for that of $\chi_\alpha$, and put $a_{\alpha i}:=\langle\rho_\alpha u_{\alpha i},u_{\alpha i}\rangle$. By [F4], the block-$\alpha$ eigenvalues of $K_{\sigma_A}:=-\log\sigma_A$ on $u_{\alpha i}\otimes v_{\alpha j}$ are $-\log q_\alpha-\log t_{\alpha i}-\log c_{\alpha j}$; the diagonal entries of $\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha$ in that basis are $a_{\alpha i}c_{\alpha j}$. Its block trace against $K_{\sigma_A}$ is therefore $p_\alpha\sum_{i,j}a_{\alpha i}c_{\alpha j}(-\log q_\alpha-\log t_{\alpha i}-\log c_{\alpha j})$. Factoring the finite sums and using $\sum_i a_{\alpha i}=\operatorname{tr}\rho_\alpha=1$, $\sum_jc_{\alpha j}=1$, $\sum_i a_{\alpha i}(-\log t_{\alpha i})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\alpha(-\log\sigma_\alpha))$, and $-\sum_jc_{\alpha j}\log c_{\alpha j}=s(\chi_\alpha)$, summing over $\alpha$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_AK_{\sigma_A})=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha[-\log q_\alpha+\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\alpha(-\log\sigma_\alpha))+s(\chi_\alpha)]$.

By [F1] and faithfulness from step 1.1, $D(\rho_A\|\sigma_A)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_AK_{\sigma_A})-s(\rho_A)$, since $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_AK_{\sigma_A})=s(\sigma_A)$ by the spectral entropy definition. Applying the same identity [F1] sectorwise gives $D(\rho_\alpha\|\sigma_\alpha)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\alpha(-\log\sigma_\alpha))-s(\rho_\alpha)$. Subtract the entropy expression in step 2.1 from the trace expression in step 2.2; the ancillary terms cancel and $-\sum_\alpha p_\alpha\log q_\alpha-H(\mathbf p)=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha\log(p_\alpha/q_\alpha)$. This is the claimed relative-entropy identity.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set. For each $\alpha\in I$, let $H_\alpha,K_\alpha$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. A density matrix is a self-adjoint endomorphism with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one; it is faithful when all its eigenvalues are strictly positive. Let $p_\alpha,q_\alpha>0$ with $\sum_\alpha p_\alpha=\sum_\alpha q_\alpha=1$, let $\rho_\alpha$ be a density matrix on $H_\alpha$, let $\sigma_\alpha$ be a faithful density matrix on $H_\alpha$, and let $\chi_\alpha$ be a fixed faithful density matrix on $K_\alpha$. Form the finite orthogonal direct sums

$$\rho_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha,\qquad \sigma_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}q_\alpha\sigma_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha.$$

For a density matrix $\tau$, set $s(\tau):=-\sum_{\lambda_j(\tau)>0}\lambda_j(\tau)\log\lambda_j(\tau)$, with $0\log0:=0$, so entropy is in nats.
